title: Summer memory trail
language: I visited… / First… Then… Finally…
model: Last summer, Salma visited her cousins. First, they walked to the park. Then, they played a ball game. Finally, they went home.
question: What happened before the ball game?
key: They walked to the park.
task: Give each partner two different story cards: A has visited cousins and went home; B has walked to the park and played a ball game. Keep cards private. Describe the events and agree an order. Place four markers in order and walk the route together, saying the story. Reveal and compare cards; swap storyteller and walker.
outcome: A four-event spoken story in a jointly agreed order.

title: Holiday listening detectives
language: Where did…? / What did…? / on Saturday
model: On Saturday, Youssef visited a park in Rabat. He played football with his cousins. On Sunday, he stayed at home and drew a picture.
question: Where did Youssef go on Saturday, and what did he do on Sunday?
key: A park in Rabat; he stayed home and drew a picture.
task: Reader A privately receives the Saturday sentences; reader B receives the Sunday sentences. Read to a partner who has two blank day cards. The listener moves each card to a park or home station using what they hear, then asks a clarification question. Swap roles with the two days. Read the complete text to check the reconstructed weekend.
outcome: Two correct day–place–action matches and one clarification question.

title: Past-tense action gallery
language: visited / played / walked / stayed
model: I played volleyball on Monday. My friend walked to the library on Tuesday. We stayed at home on Wednesday.
question: Which verbs describe completed past activities?
key: Played, walked and stayed.
task: A privately chooses Monday or Tuesday; B privately chooses home or school as a new place. Share the missing information and create three past-tense sentences about a fictional weekend. Mime each chosen activity slowly while a checker writes the sentence. Compare the written verbs to the language strip; rotate roles.
outcome: Three original past-tense sentences matched to three mimes.

title: A postcard in four moves
language: First / Then / After that / Finally
model: Hello Sami! I am back from my holiday. First, I visited my aunt. Then, we walked by the sea. After that, we played a game. Finally, I returned home. From Lina.
question: Find four words or phrases that organise the events.
key: First; Then; After that; Finally.
task: A holds event cards visited aunt and returned home. B holds walked by the sea and played a game. Orally agree an order without showing cards. Build four frozen poses, one per event, and explain the sequence. Each learner writes an original 40–60 word postcard, then swaps it for a check of sequence words and past verbs.
outcome: An original 40–60 word postcard with a clear sequence.

title: Find your school club
language: I enjoy… / You could join… / because…
model: A: I enjoy drawing and making posters. B: You could join the art club because you like creative work. A: When does it meet? B: On Tuesday.
question: Which club does B recommend, and why?
key: The art club, because A likes creative work.
task: Set three club stations: art Tuesday, reading Thursday and sports Friday. A has a preference card (drawing, stories or ball games); B has the private club timetable. Interview each other and select a club that matches the preference. Walk or point to the chosen station and explain the choice. Swap cards and roles.
outcome: A suitable club recommendation with a reason and meeting day.

title: Club experience interviews
language: Have you ever…? / Yes, I have. / No, I haven’t.
model: A: Have you ever made a poster? B: Yes, I have. A: Have you ever acted in a play? B: No, I haven’t.
question: Which experience has B had?
key: Making a poster.
task: Use fictional role cards: A has made a poster but never acted; B has acted but never made a poster. Keep roles private and interview each other. For every yes answer, place an experience token at the correct picture station. Compare the completed two-column interview chart with the hidden cards and switch roles.
outcome: Two accurate interview answers recorded for a fictional learner.

title: Build an inclusive team
language: patient / helpful / creative / reliable
model: Amal listens before she speaks. Idriss brings the equipment on time. Hiba draws clear posters. All three help the club in different ways.
question: Who would be a useful equipment checker? Give evidence.
key: Idriss: he brings equipment on time. Other reasoned roles are possible.
task: A reads the first and last sentences; B reads the middle two. Exchange evidence to assign guide, equipment checker and poster maker. Model each role through one gentle movement task: guide a token route, check three paper markers, display a poster. Rotate roles so everyone experiences a different responsibility. Explain one assignment using evidence.
outcome: A justified role plan with one supporting detail per assignment.

title: Spend the club budget
language: Let’s choose… / How much…? / We can afford…
model: The club has 60 imaginary dirhams. A ball costs 30. A set of markers costs 20. A poster pack costs 15.
question: Can the club buy all three items?
key: No: 30 + 20 + 15 = 65, which exceeds 60.
task: A privately holds the prices; B holds the 60-dirham budget and goal: a game for six learners with a clear playing area. Ask for prices and negotiate a purchase. Use paper tokens, never real money. Set out the chosen paper equipment symbols and demonstrate the planned game with comfortable steps or hand movements. Explain the cost and one compromise.
outcome: A feasible equipment plan within 60 imaginary dirhams.

title: Invite a friend to sports day
language: Would you like to…? / I’d love to. / Sorry, I can’t.
model: A: Would you like to come to our sports day on Friday? B: I’d love to. What time does it start? A: At three o’clock.
question: What details does the invitation give?
key: Sports day; Friday; three o’clock.
task: A privately holds sports day Friday at three and reading day Thursday at two. B holds availability: free Thursday at two, busy Friday at three. Invite, accept or politely decline, and find a workable event. Walk or point to the event station only after both confirm day and time. Swap availability cards and roles.
outcome: An invitation exchange ending in a feasible agreed event.

title: Plan a celebration together
language: Let’s… / How about…? / That’s a good idea.
model: A: Let’s organise a class celebration. B: How about a poster corner and a team game? A: That’s a good idea. We need enough space for everyone.
question: Which two activities are suggested?
key: A poster corner and a team game.
task: A has available resources: paper, markers and a soft ball. B has constraints: 20 minutes, no food, everyone needs a meaningful role. Share the private cards and choose two activities. Use floor or desk markers to demonstrate a route between them. Agree who welcomes, explains and checks; rotate these roles.
outcome: A two-activity celebration plan meeting all shared constraints.

title: Celebration listening route
language: on Monday / at two / in the hall
model: The school celebration is on Monday at two o’clock. The art display is in the hall. The team game is in the playground. Bring a paper invitation.
question: Where is the art display and what should visitors bring?
key: In the hall; a paper invitation.
task: Reader A has the first two sentences and reader B the last two. Listeners receive hall and playground picture markers, a blank event card and no script. Exchange information orally, place activity cards at the correct stations, and guide a partner through the visitor route. Read the full script afterward to check details.
outcome: A correct visitor route and event card with day, time and needed item.

title: Write an event invitation
language: You are invited… / on… / at… / Please bring…
model: You are invited to our class game afternoon on Wednesday at two o’clock in the school hall. Please bring a pencil. We hope to see you there!
question: Identify the event, day, time, place and item.
key: Game afternoon; Wednesday; two o’clock; school hall; pencil.
task: A receives event and place (team challenge, playground); B receives day, time and item (Thursday, three o’clock, water bottle). Share the missing information and rehearse a visitor’s route using two markers. Each learner writes an original invitation with all five details. Swap and check completeness; offer a spoken version for learners needing writing support.
outcome: A complete original invitation with five practical details.

title: Invention clue trail
language: It is used for… / It helps people…
model: A bicycle helps people travel. It has two wheels and uses no fuel while you pedal. A lamp helps people see when a room is dark.
question: Which object needs pedalling, and which helps in a dark room?
key: Bicycle; lamp.
task: A privately holds picture cards for bicycle, lamp and umbrella. B holds clues: two wheels and pedal; gives light; keeps rain off. Read and describe without showing cards. Move matching picture tokens to clue stations and explain the evidence. Swap clue reader and mover; verify all three matches together.
outcome: Three justified object–function matches.

title: Inventor interview studio
language: What does it do? / How does it work? / Who can use it?
model: Reporter: What does your imaginary invention do? Inventor: It sorts paper for reuse. Reporter: How does it work? Inventor: You turn a handle.
question: Is this invention real or imaginary, and what does it do?
key: Imaginary; it sorts paper for reuse.
task: A invents a fictional sports-equipment organiser using a private drawing; B has three interview questions but cannot see the drawing. Interview, then B mimes how the imagined device works and sketches it. Reveal and compare the sketch with A’s drawing. Repair one misunderstanding and swap roles. Do not claim a real inventor created this fictional device.
outcome: A three-question interview and a checked reconstruction of an imaginary invention.

title: Then and now in motion
language: used to… / now…
model: In this fictional school, learners used to copy every notice by hand. Now they read notices on a shared screen. They still ask questions and help each other.
question: What changed and what stayed the same?
key: Notices changed from hand-copying to a shared screen; asking questions and helping continued.
task: A holds a then card: hand-written notices and paper maps. B holds a now card: shared screen and digital map. Compare information without showing cards. Create two frozen scenes, past and present, and describe each contrast with used to and now. Reveal cards, verify the contrasts, and discuss one thing that should stay unchanged: cooperation.
outcome: Two accurate past–present comparisons about the fictional school.

title: Design a useful invention
language: Our invention helps… / It has… / You can…
model: Our imaginary ball carrier helps a team collect soft balls. It has a wide bag and two handles. Two learners carry it together at walking pace.
question: What is the invention’s purpose and how is it carried?
key: To collect soft balls; two learners carry it together at walking pace.
task: A has the problem: loose equipment after a game. B has design limits: paper prototype only, no electricity, everyone can explain one part. Negotiate an imaginary solution. Build a paper sketch and mime its use without constructing or testing machinery. Write a 40–60 word description covering purpose, parts and use; exchange for an evidence-based check.
outcome: An original labelled sketch and short description of a fictional invention.

title: Future careers interview
language: I’d like to… / because… / What skills…?
model: A: I’d like to be a sports coach because I enjoy helping a team. B: What skills do you need? A: Clear communication and patience.
question: What reason and two skills does A give?
key: Enjoys helping a team; clear communication and patience.
task: A holds a fictional interest card (helping teams, drawing or caring for animals); B holds job cards (coach, designer, vet) with skill clues. Interview to find a suitable match. Mime one safe job-related gesture at the selected picture station, then justify the match with two clues. Swap roles; accept different matches when the reasons fit.
outcome: A career recommendation supported by an interest and a relevant skill.

title: Our next team challenge
language: We are going to… / We need to… / First…
model: We are going to organise a walking treasure hunt. First, we need to write clues. Then, we need to mark a clear route. Finally, we will test the clues together.
question: What must the team do before testing the clues?
key: Write clues and mark a clear route.
task: A has route requirements: start by the door, visit two paper cones, finish at the desk. B has task requirements: ask a question at each cone, no running, everyone gives a clue. Negotiate a plan, set paper markers and test the route. Give a short going-to report, then revise one unclear instruction.
outcome: A tested route and three-sentence future plan meeting both sets of requirements.

title: Read our future-choice survey
language: more than / fewer than / the same number
model: In a fictional survey of 12 learners, 5 chose a sports club, 4 chose an art club and 3 chose a reading club. Each learner chose one club.
question: Which club is most popular, and how many more chose sports than reading?
key: Sports; two more learners.
task: A holds sports 5 and art 4; B holds reading 3 and total 12. Exchange the missing figures, then build a floor or desk bar chart using twelve paper tokens. Walk along or trace each bar and state two comparisons. Check that the total is 12. Choose one club event using the data and explain why minority choices still matter.
outcome: A correct three-bar token chart with two comparisons and a reasoned event choice.

title: A goal and a next step
language: I will… / I might… / My next step is…
model: My goal is to speak more English in team activities. I will learn two useful phrases this week. I might practise with a friend after class. My next step is to make a phrase card.
question: Which plan is definite, which is possible, and what is the next step?
key: Will learn two phrases: definite plan; might practise: possibility; make a phrase card: next step.
task: A privately chooses a fictional learning goal (clear directions or confident questions). B holds support options (phrase card, partner rehearsal, teacher model). Share information and select a suitable support. Rehearse a three-marker route: goal, action, check. Each learner writes a personal or fictional four-sentence plan using will, might and one achievable next step.
outcome: A four-sentence plan with a goal, a definite action, a possibility and a next step.
